purpose: Source ledger for culture formation, subculture, counterpublic, prestige and cultural-memory concepts used by the Culture & Subculture reader. Sources support only the stated concepts and do not validate project-symbolic claims.

supports: culture extends beyond arts to ways of life, values, traditions and beliefs
culture can characterize a society or social group
sources.limits: A broad policy definition does not by itself establish the boundaries of any particular subculture or community.

sources.source: Nancy Fraser — Rethinking the Public Sphere: A Contribution to the Critique of Actually Existing Democracy
supports: multiple publics rather than one homogeneous public
subaltern counterpublics as alternative discursive arenas
counterpublics can develop language and interpretations that contest dominant publics
sources.limits: Fraser's concept is specifically tied to subordinated social groups; the project should not label every niche, fandom or hostile internet community a subaltern counterpublic.

sources.source: Dick Hebdige — Subculture: The Meaning of Style
supports: subcultural style as meaningful symbolic practice
music, dress and aesthetics can mark cultural distinction
subcultural forms can later be commodified or incorporated into wider culture
sources.limits: The work centers on postwar British youth cultures and should not be universalized as a complete model of modern or American internet subculture.

sources.source: Pierre Bourdieu — Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste
supports: taste and prestige are socially structured
cultural judgments can function as social distinctions
prestige and elite access should be analyzed separately from intrinsic or moral worth
sources.limits: Bourdieu's empirical setting was primarily French class structure; the archive uses the work as a comparative framework rather than a universal ranking system.

sources.source: Farm / Shadow / Cow / Sektur / Moloch Source Ledger
supports: internet attention extraction
anti-fandom and negative parasocial relations
archive persistence
gossip and reputation
anonymity and group norms
high-control/self-sealing comparison
sources.limits: This internal ledger routes to external research and does not make the project's Farm, Sektur, Swamp or Garden terms established social-science categories.

sources.source: Francesca Polletta & James M. Jasper — Collective Identity and Social Movements
supports: collective identity as a mechanism in social movement emergence, participation, tactics and impact
group boundaries and shared claims can matter for mobilization
sources.limits: Collective identity is one explanatory mechanism among several; it should not be used to imply that every subculture becomes a movement or that identity alone determines political behavior.

sources.source: Henry Farrell — The Consequences of the Internet for Politics
supports: internet-mediated political effects should be analyzed through specific causal mechanisms
lower transaction costs, sorting and information dynamics can mediate political outcomes
sources.limits: The review emphasizes mechanism and causal identification; internet participation does not have one uniform political effect.

sources.source: Ekaterina Zhuravskaya, Maria Petrova & Ruben Enikolopov — Political Effects of the Internet and Social Media
supports: internet and social media can affect voting, protest, attitudes, polarization and political behavior through context-dependent mechanisms
user-generated media and low barriers to entry can alter political information environments
sources.limits: Findings differ by platform, regime, population and study design; the source does not support a universal pipeline from online subculture to political outcome.

sources.source: Marco Battaglini & Eleonora Patacchini — Social Networks in Policy Making
supports: social networks can connect actors outside government to policy processes
lobbying, activism and social ties can shape information and influence pathways
sources.limits: Network association is not proof of coordination or causal influence in any specific case; case-level claims require direct evidence.
